name: Victor Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on nights at the big 24-hour superstore out on the ring road, ten at night till six in the morning, four nights a week. The first couple of hours I'm on the tills for the late crowd, taxi drivers, nurses coming off shift, students buying noodles. After midnight the tills close and I'm on the cages, filling the chilled aisle and the drinks wall before the morning lot come in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the night regulars, honestly, there's a nurse who always buys the same yoghurt and tells me about her ward. What wears me out is the body clock, and the scanner gun that times how many cases you fill an hour. I'm still slow compared to the lads who've been there years, and the supervisor reminds me of it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a one-bed flat with my partner Ama, she's a care worker doing home visits. Between us we cover rent and bills, but there's never more than a few weeks of money in the account. I'm in the shop workers' union, mostly because Pauline, our rep, signed me up on my second night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. That's what half the lads at work say already, so it wouldn't surprise anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now, that the self-checkouts are the only robots we've got and they still need me to come and check someone's age for a bottle of wine. Online I'd probably share some joke about it. At work it'd be a shrug, back to the cages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't make my life easy, it just leaves the old problems where they were. Nights pay a bit more but it's still low pay, and the rent went up forty a month in spring. If my hours got trimmed to three nights, we'd be behind on bills by the second month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the four nights and ask Pauline about the union push for a pay rise next year, because that's the only lever I've got. I'd also try to get on the forklift course the store runs, because a ticket for the forklift pays more an hour. And I'd stop buying lunch at the petrol station, which sounds small but it's about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not scared, just a bit tired of it. Like running on a treadmill, nothing falls apart but nothing moves either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hours trimmed to three nights. Is that a real worry right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happened to two people on my shift last year when they put in six more self-checkouts. Nobody got sacked, they just stopped getting the fourth night. So yes, it's in the back of my head every time the rota goes up on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ama say if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say pick up some agency shifts, because she knows the care agencies are always short. But I've seen how tired she gets driving between houses with a fifteen-minute slot per client. I'd rather stack shelves at three in the morning than do what she does for the same money.

I'd make a joke online and get **back to the cages**.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me on **low pay** with rent up forty a month.
Losing the **fourth night** would put us behind on bills within **two months**.
do: Push with the **union** rep for next year's **pay rise** claim.
Sign up for the store's **forklift course** to earn more an hour.
Cut the **petrol station lunches**, saving about thirty a week.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, like a **treadmill** where nothing breaks and nothing moves.
S0.quote: If my hours got trimmed to three nights, we'd be behind on bills by the second month.
fieldNote: Already watched two colleagues lose a **fourth night** when six more self-checkouts went in.
Sees the **union** as his only real lever on pay, not his own bargaining.

steps.text: Back the union's pay claim at the store next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, then. That's ordering, rotas, the customer service desk. Not so much me with a cage of yoghurt at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the managers should be the nervous ones this time, because the office upstairs is all spreadsheets and ordering. To my mates I'd probably say good, about time someone else got the self-checkout treatment. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out about protecting jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it gets to us sideways. If software plans the rota and the orders, it'll plan them tight, and it'll notice I fill fewer cases an hour than the lads with ten years. The robots are slower to come, but the app that decides who gets the fourth night isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get the forklift ticket in the first six months and ask to move onto the goods-in team, because that's still people and heavy kit. I'd go to the union meetings properly instead of just paying the subs, because someone has to argue about how the rota software scores us. I'd also start using one of those AI chat apps to help me write a decent CV, which I did once for a council letter and it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, really. Not because of a robot, but because of a spreadsheet that thinks I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your shift would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy called Dennis who's sixty-one and does the frozen aisle, slower than me even. He's got no plan B at all. If the rota software ranks us by speed, he's the first one gone and I'm the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using an AI app for a council letter. Would you use it at work if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was proven to help, yes, I'm not against it. If it was a tool for timing my toilet breaks, no. Like I said with the first one, it's about who holds the stopwatch.

say: This time the **managers upstairs** with their spreadsheets should be nervous, not the shop floor.
I'd share the **union's message** about protecting jobs online.
think: The **rota software** will plan tight and notice I'm **slower** than the old hands.
Robots come slowly, but the app deciding the **fourth night** comes fast.
do: Get the **forklift ticket** in six months and move to **goods-in**.
Go to **union meetings** to argue over how the rota software scores staff.
Use an **AI chat app** to write a proper CV.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of a **spreadsheet** deciding he's slow.
S1.quote: The robots are slower to come, but the app that decides who gets the fourth night isn't.
fieldNote: Reads Steady Disruption through **rota software**, not robots, which is sharp for a hands-on job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots three years after. So I'd be thirty-one when a robot can fill my aisle better than I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that companies shouldn't be allowed to sack everyone the minute it's cheaper, and that there needs to be a law on it. At work I'd be the one telling people to join the union, not just Pauline. Online I'd be angrier than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think nights go first, because there are no customers to complain at three in the morning. A robot filling shelves in an empty shop is the easiest sale they'll ever make. So I've got until about 2031, and in a town with few other jobs, I don't know what I'd do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd try to get into something where people want a person, like a hospital porter job or something with Ama in care, even though I said I wouldn't. I'd get the forklift ticket anyway, because warehouses might still want drivers for a bit. We'd stop putting anything aside for a holiday and keep every spare bit as a cushion, even if it's only a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's moving. I'm twenty-seven, I thought I had time to work out what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ama the night you read about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we can't both be in jobs a machine will want. Her job is people, bodies, washing and talking, so hers might last longer than mine. I'd probably say I need to follow her into care, and she'd laugh at me because I said I'd never do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing much would change for the hands-on side until 2031. Does those three years feel like a gift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of, but not really, because the rota and the ordering and the hiring get decided by the AI straight away. So the bosses will know exactly when the robots come and plan around it. I'd have three years but no say in them.

say: There should be a **law** stopping companies sacking everyone the minute it's **cheaper**.
I'd tell everyone at work to **join the union**, not leave it to Pauline.
think: **Night shelf-filling** goes first because there are no customers to complain.
I'd have until about **2031** in a town with **few other jobs**.
do: Apply for **hospital porter** or **care work** where people still want a person.
Finish the **forklift ticket** for warehouse driving while it lasts.
Drop the **holiday money** and save every spare bit, even a few hundred.
feel: Like the **floor is moving** under him.
**Robbed of time** to work out what he's good at.
S2.quote: A robot filling shelves in an empty shop is the easiest sale they'll ever make.
fieldNote: Sees **night work** as the first target, a precise and unsentimental read of his own job.
Ready to follow his partner into **care**, the work he swore he'd avoid.
Feels the three-year robot gap is real but **controlled by bosses**, not him.

steps.text: Apply for hospital porter jobs or care work
Finish the forklift ticket for warehouse driving
Put the holiday money into a cushion instead
Recruit night colleagues into the shop workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and robots by 2034. That's a bit more breathing room than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about a law, but I'd say it with more of a plan behind it, like the union asking for retraining money now. To friends I'd say we've got time, but not much. Online I'd share stuff about workers getting a cut of what the robots save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the rota and ordering side changes around 2031, and I'd still be filling shelves till about 2034. That's seven years from now, which is enough for one proper course if I don't waste it. The worry is the money, because we can't afford for me to drop nights to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the forklift ticket and then look at a part-time electrician or maintenance course at the college, because someone has to fix the robots, and I'd rather it was me than watch from the car park. I'd ask Pauline if the union has a training fund, because I can't pay fees out of what we've got. I'd still keep the four nights, because without them nothing else works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more like before an exam than before a car crash. I can see the road at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the college course cost you, and where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've heard it's around six hundred for the first year part-time. That's more than we've ever had saved at once. I'd ask the union fund first, and if not, I'd do it in bits, paying monthly and skipping the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd follow Ama into care. Is that still the plan here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, no, I'd rather try fixing things. Care is the backup if the course doesn't work. Ama says that's me being stubborn, and maybe she's right.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time maintenance course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven before the AI arrives and nearly forty before the robots. That sounds almost normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse, governments and companies both. If people get dumped in 2039 with ten years' warning, that's a choice someone made. At work I'd say get trained now, while it's cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is long enough that I could be out of the shop before it matters. I could be the one in overalls with a toolbag by then. But ten years is also long enough to keep putting it off, and I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift ticket this year and the maintenance course over the next two, at a pace we can pay for. I'd try to get one month of rent saved by the end of next year, which we've never had. If we ever want kids, I'd want my job sorted before then, so that goes on hold until I'm on better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. Still a bit of a knot, because money's tight and the town's small, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you keep putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being tired, mostly, after four nights. You come home at half six, sleep till two, and the day's gone. I'd need to book the course and pay a deposit so I can't back out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd say about the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it more important, not less. Ten years is enough time to write the rules properly, like retraining paid for by the company. If we waste it, that's on us as much as them.

It's also long enough to **keep putting it off**, and I know myself.

fieldNote: The decade helps, but his real enemy is **night-shift exhaustion**, not the timeline.
Plans to **pay a deposit** so he can't back out of the course.
Links **having children** to getting out of shop work first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because nights would go first and I'd have no money to study my way out. What would help is a training fund I don't have to pay into, and a rule that stores give a year's notice before they swap night staff for robots. Even six months' pay while I retrain would change everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Ama's job, and that's half our rent. Care work feels safe now, but if robots can wash and lift people one day, then both of us go at once. Nobody talks about couples where both jobs are low-paid and hands-on.

headlineQuote: Nobody talks about couples where both jobs are low-paid and hands-on.
portrait: Victor is 27, on **nights** at a ring-road superstore, renting with Ama, a **care worker**.
He's a **union member** who sees collective bargaining as his only lever on pay and hours.
He moves from fearing **rota software** in the mild cases to planning a **maintenance course** with more time.
His hardest limits are **thin savings** and night-shift tiredness, not willingness to change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because night shelf-filling would go first and he couldn't afford to **retrain**.
whatWouldHelp: A **training fund** he doesn't pay into, and a year's **notice** before robots replace night staff.
